reasoning: Form V verb (ta3awwad in formal speech). Colloquial Palestinian usually takes the it- prefix: it3awwad, with doubled w. I spelled it with the alif to match. The it- versus ta- choice is the uncertain part.

The he-form present with the bi- prefix is biDghaT, with emphatic ض. 3aleena is the Palestinian form of 'on us'. The written ي of بيضغط is dropped in the vowelling so a TTS voice does not read a long vowel.
3ushb is understood and used for grass, herbs and weeds. Everyday Palestinian for lawn or field grass is 7ashiish. The vowel of 3ushb is the uncertain part.
keef is the Palestinian 'how'. The hamza after the article is written inside the token: il-'ahl. 'Keef il-3eyle' is an equally common alternative.
Taa marbuta after د is e, not a. Long aa after ع. Everyday word for habit or custom; 3aadatan or 3aade also means 'usually'.
The article assimilates to ش: ish-shaam. This is the standard term for the Levant, shared across the region. In speech ish-shaam alone can also mean Syria or Damascus.
ط is emphatic, so T. ق is a glottal stop in this word as spoken in everyday use; the formal reading would keep [q]. Palestinians also often just say 'app'.
Palestinian for fingernail is Dufur with emphatic ض, not MSA Dhufr. It also covers toenails. The epenthetic vowel is the uncertain part.
The spelling معك is the same for masculine ma3ak and feminine ma3ik. The English says 'to f.', so I used ma3ik. A common Palestinian goodbye.
Form II with a doubled j: ajjar means to rent out to someone. The tenant's verb is ista'jar. Word-initial hamza is only a vowel seat, so it is not written.
In speech the final hamza of عزاء is normally dropped, giving il-3aza for the mourning gathering. Condolences themselves are often ta3ziye. The formal 3azaa' is possible but less typical.
English loanword, usually stressed on the first syllable with a long aa. The vowel length of the first syllable is the uncertain part, since the given spelling has no alif.
Geographic proper noun. ق keeps [q] in afriiqya, as in other proper nouns. The phrase is a construct with no article.
ح is 7, ص is the emphatic S. The first vowel is a short i. The standard everyday word for horse.
Doubled k, long aa, and taa marbuta after ن is e. A small shop or kiosk; dukkaan is the plain form.
Taa marbuta after ي is e, so baamye. Common Palestinian word for okra, often cooked with tomato and meat.
Doubled y, with the stress on the middle syllable. Commonly used alone for an air conditioner.
Form V from an MSA root. In urban speech ث usually becomes s in such words, so ta'assar, with the hamza written as '. A t or th variant is possible, which is why confidence is medium.
Colloquial reduction of li'anna, with the final -o of inno. The hamza is medial here, so it is written: la'inno. The first vowel can also be heard as li-.
ح is 7. The hamza of ahliyye starts a separate word, so it is only a vowel seat. The ـية ending has doubled y, with e for taa marbuta.
Everyday word, so ق is a glottal stop. Taa marbuta after ل is e. 3ashiire (clan) is also common.
Idiom meaning 'the chance went by me'. علي is 3aliyy with doubled y, the colloquial form of 3alayya. The vowel quality before the doubled y is the uncertain part.
A proper noun that Palestinians use in conversation and news. Doubled t, ح is 7, and taa marbuta after د is e. The hamza after il- is written inside the token.
English loanword with a long ii and initial sp-. The Arabic spelling uses ب for p; many speakers say sbiikar. The formal alternative is mukabbir Sawt.
Standard loanword for petrol, with a long ii in the stressed last syllable.
